issues.legal_issue: A party who withdraws the purchase price deposited under a pre-emption decree is not thereby barred from pursuing an appeal challenging that decree when the withdrawal is compensation for the loss of the property and does not amount to accepting a separate benefit under the decree.
material_facts: A decree in a pre-emption suit allowed the pre-emptor to acquire the property by depositing the purchase price within the time fixed by the court.
The purchaser challenged the decree by appeal, and special leave to appeal was granted on a constitutional ground.
The pre-emptor deposited the purchase price as required, and the purchaser withdrew it from court.
The purchaser’s withdrawal of the price was treated as compensation for the loss of the property, rather than as a benefit independent of the merits of the claim.
The withdrawal did not make restitution impossible or inequitable, and the purchaser had no choice between alternative rights.
issues.conclusion: The withdrawal did not amount to adoption of the decree or forfeit the purchaser’s statutory right of appeal; the preliminary objection was overruled and the appeal could proceed.
issues.legal_principle: The doctrine against approbating and reprobating does not ordinarily bar a statutory appeal merely because a party has received something under a judgment. It applies where the party has elected to take a benefit independent of the merits of the claim and cannot accept that benefit while repudiating a dependent part of the order. Whether post-judgment conduct bars an appeal also depends on whether it creates actual inconsistency, including whether restitution has become impossible or inequitable and whether the party had alternative rights from which to choose. The Court relied on Tinkler v. Hilder (1849) 4 Ex. 187, Verschu(re)s Creameries v. Hull and Netherlands Steamship Co. [1921] 2 K.B. 608, Lissenden v. C. A. V. Bosch Ltd. [1940] A.C. 412, Venkatarayudu v. Chinna, A.I.R. 1930 Mad. 268, and Sundra Das v. Dhanpat Rai, 1907 P.R. No. 16. No statutory provision or recognised equitable principle was shown to deprive the appellant of the right of appeal.

rule.if: preemption_decree_appeal and appellant_withdrew_deposited_purchase_price and withdrawn_price_was_compensation_for_property_loss and not withdrawal_made_restitution_impossible_or_inequitable and no_alternative_rights_were_available

predicates.preemption_decree_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a decree that permits one party to acquire property by paying a purchase price to the other.
predicates.appellant_withdrew_deposited_purchase_pr: The party challenging the decree withdrew the purchase price deposited under it.
predicates.withdrawn_price_was_compensation_for_pro: The withdrawn sum compensated the recipient for the loss of the property rather than giving the recipient a separate benefit independent of the claim’s merits.
predicates.withdrawal_made_restitution_impossible_o: The withdrawal made it impossible or inequitable to restore the parties if the decree were later set aside.
predicates.no_alternative_rights_were_available: The party had no alternative rights or remedies between which the party could elect.

issues.definition: When a party in an appeal from a pre-emption decree withdraws the deposited price as compensation for property loss, and the withdrawal neither prevents fair restitution nor reflects a choice between alternative rights, the appeal may proceed.
